excerpt: Checking a school, exam, or admission result on the official portal: the details to have ready, why the page times out, and the print copy to keep.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to check a result or an admission status online, on the official page, without paying anybody for a free link. You will have the details ready, handle a page that times out, and keep a printed copy.
Result portals are slow on the day results are released, because thousands of people open them at once. Knowing that in advance prevents most of the panic.
Before you start

items: The candidate's registration number or index number.
The exam year or session, exactly as written on the slip.
A phone or computer, and data, with the battery charged.
Ten minutes, and the patience for a page that may need a second try.

body.text: Find the real portal

items: Search for the exam body or the institution by name.
Read the address before clicking, since official pages use a government or institution domain.
Ignore any result-checking site that asks for a payment to a personal account.
Bookmark the page once you are sure of it.
Have the school's phone number ready, in case the portal is down completely.
Ask a teacher or the school office for the exact portal address, which they use themselves.

body.text: You will see the official page carry a crest, a plain layout, and a form with two or three fields. A page with more advertisements than fields is not the portal.

body.alt: A phone showing a results portal with fields for an index number and a PIN.
body.caption: Two fields, usually the index number and a PIN or a session. The official page is plain, and the form is small.

body.text: It looks like paying an agent is the only way to get the result quickly. The portal is free to check, and the agent is charging for a page you can open yourself.
When the page will not load

items: Try again after fifteen minutes, since the first hour is the busiest.
Check the number and the session before assuming the site is broken.
Look at the error message: wrong details and a busy server give different messages.
Use a different network if the page fails completely, since one provider may be blocked.
Write the number on paper first, so a mistake in typing shows at once.
Keep the page open once it loads, and take a screenshot before refreshing.

body.text: The result page will usually show the candidate's name, the subjects or the course, and the status in large text. Read the name first, since a wrong result for the right number is a common and frightening surprise.

body.alt: A printed result slip on a table beside a phone showing the same page.
body.caption: Print two copies: one for the file, one to carry. A screenshot on a phone is not a document an office will accept.

body.text: Keep a copy that lasts

items: Screenshot the page with the address bar visible, which shows where it came from.
Save it as a PDF, or print it at a business centre.
Keep the printed copy in the envelope with the certificates.
Photograph the printout and upload it to the folder of documents from an earlier lesson.
Note the date and time of the check, in case of a later dispute.
Check again the next day to confirm the result has not changed.

body.text: None of this needs an office visit. A printed copy, a photograph of it, and a folder are enough to prove what the page said.
Do not worry about checking on the first morning. The result is the same at noon, and the portal is readable then.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a route, and the school or the exam body is the authority.

items: The details are rejected: check the session year first, which is the usual error.
The result is not the expected one: confirm the name and the number, then contact the school.
The page asks for a card payment: stop, and check with the school before paying anything.
The server is completely down: call the school office, which often has a list.
The portal asked for a PIN you do not have: ask the school where the PIN is issued.
You lost the printed copy: check the portal again, and print two this time.

body.text: Practice
Do the preparation before the result is released.

items: Write the registration number and session on paper.
Find the official portal and bookmark it.
Test that the page opens, without entering details.
Save the school's phone number in contacts.
Decide where the printed copy will be kept.

body.text: You can now check a result yourself, without paying for the privilege. In the next lesson you will set the family rules around phones and children.

excerpt: Setting up a child's phone or tablet safely: the controls worth turning on, the conversations that matter more, and where the device should sleep.

body.text: This lesson is about phones, tablets, and children in one household. You will set the controls that matter, agree house rules everybody understands, and decide where devices sleep at night.
Parental controls are useful and limited. They cannot replace a conversation, and a child who understands the reason follows a rule more reliably than one who only meets a lock.
Before you start

items: The child's device, and the account it uses.
Twenty minutes, and the child in the room if they are old enough to talk to.
A charging spot outside the bedrooms.

body.text: The controls worth turning on

items: A screen lock with a PIN that you also know.
The app store set to ask for approval before any install or purchase.
Family Link on Android, or Screen Time on an iPhone, set up under your account.
Ages set correctly on the child's account, which limits what appears in stores.
Location sharing with a parent, if the child travels alone.
Automatic updates on, since an old app is where most trouble starts.

body.text: You will see a weekly report listing the time spent in each app, which is more useful than an argument about how long they have been on the phone. Read it together, rather than in secret.

body.alt: A parent's phone showing a child's app usage and time limits.
body.caption: A weekly report, read together. The figure settles the argument faster than either person's memory.

body.text: It looks like a setting can make the internet safe. Settings filter some of it, and the rest is handled by rules, by trust, and by the child knowing they can tell you something bad happened.
Rules everybody can say

items: No devices at the table, for the adults as well.
Devices charge in the living room, not beside the bed.
Strangers are not friends, even when the profile looks like a child.
Nothing about where the child lives or goes to school is posted.
If something frightening appears, tell an adult, with no punishment attached.
Screen time ends at a fixed hour, agreed in advance.

body.text: None of these need an app to enforce. A charger in the living room does more than a dozen blocked sites.
Do not worry about being strict or lenient enough. Consistency matters more than severity, and a rule that adults also follow survives.

body.alt: A child typing on a laptop with an adult sitting beside them.
body.caption: Sitting beside, not behind. The adult who was there for the first week is the one the child tells about the strange message.

body.text: The conversation that does the work
Explain what the controls are for, in the same way you would explain a bicycle helmet.

items: Say plainly what the app tracks, and why.
Ask what they use the phone for, and listen to the answer.
Explain that a stranger's profile can be anybody at all.
Tell them the rule about telling you, and keep the promise of no shouting.
Review the settings together every few months, as they get older.
Give more freedom at each age, rather than removing it all at once.

body.text: A child who has been warned without being frightened is safer than one who has only been blocked. The warning is what they remember when the message arrives.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is common, and the first response should be calm.

items: The child installed an app you did not approve: check the store settings, then ask what it was for.
A stranger is messaging: block and report, save the messages, and do not delete them.
The device is being used at night: move the charger, and check the weekly report.
The account was made with a false age: correct the age, which changes the content settings.
The child is being bullied: keep the messages, tell the school, and do not take the phone away as punishment.
The controls lock you out: use the family account's recovery, which is why it was set up under yours.

body.text: Practice
Set two things this week, and have one conversation.

items: Set the app store to ask for approval.
Move the charger out of the bedroom.
Show the child the weekly report and explain what it shows.
Agree the fixed hour when screens end.
Write the house rules on a card and put it where everybody sees it.

body.text: You can now hold a household together with phones in it. In the next lesson you will write a CV that a tired recruiter can read in ten seconds.

excerpt: Writing a CV a recruiter finishes: the top third that decides everything, the lines to delete, and how to tailor it to one advert in ten minutes.

body.text: This lesson shows you how to write a CV that a recruiter finishes. You will build the top third first, delete the lines that waste space, and tailor it to one advert in ten minutes.
A recruiter reads the top of the page and decides whether to read the rest. Everything that matters must be in the first three lines, above the fold on a printed page.
Before you start

items: One job advert you would actually apply for.
Your existing CV, if you have one.
About forty minutes.

body.text: The top third

items: Your name, large, at the top left.
One line under it: the job title you are applying for, not the one you have.
A phone number and an email address that use your name.
A location at city level, since employers filter by it.
Two lines of summary, naming the work you have done and the result.
Everything else comes below, and may never be read.

body.text: You will see the difference immediately when you compare your old CV with the advert. The advert names the job, and your CV should name the same job in the same words.

body.alt: A simple one-page CV on a laptop screen with clear headings.
body.caption: Plain layout, clear headings, one page. Design that hides the text costs the reader time, and the reader is tired.

body.text: It looks like a decorative CV shows effort. It shows effort to the wrong person, since the reader is scanning for a match, not admiring a border.
Lines to delete

items: A photograph, unless the advert asks for one.
Date of birth, marital status, and religion, which are not usually relevant.
A list of every school subject taken.
Hobbies with no connection to the work.
Referees whose details are already on the last page of the application form.
Phrases like hardworking and dedicated, which nobody can verify.

body.text: The page will have more white space after the deletions, which looks confident. Dense text on one page reads as a wall, and a wall is skipped.
The finished page will show the headline in one line, the summary in two, and the job you want in the words the advert used. Print it once, because paper shows what a screen hides.

body.alt: A CV draft beside a printed job advert with lines underlined.
body.caption: The advert, underlined, beside the CV. The underlined words belong in the CV, in the same form.

body.text: Experience as evidence

items: Job title, employer, and dates on one line.
Two or three lines under it, each starting with a verb.
Include numbers wherever they exist: how many, how much, how often.
Put the most relevant job first, even if it was not the most recent.
Describe unpaid work that proves the skill, such as running a family shop.
Leave out any job you cannot explain in an interview.

body.text: None of this requires a paid template. A plain document, one page, with headings for summary, experience, skills, and education, reads better than most designs.
Do not worry about gaps in your history. One line explaining a gap, such as caring for a relative or studying, is enough.
Tailoring in ten minutes

items: Copy the advert's job title into your headline.
Underline the five skills the advert names.
Check that each one appears somewhere in your CV, in their words.
Move the matching experience higher up the page.
Change the summary's second line to mention the industry.
Save it as a separate file named for that employer.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a correction, and the first is the most common.

items: No replies: the headline is generic. Change it for each advert.
The CV is two pages: cut the oldest job to one line, and delete the hobbies.
The file will not open: export as a PDF, not a photo or a document.
The recruiter asks about a skill you listed: remove it, since an interview will test it.
You have no paid experience: use unpaid work with numbers, and label it honestly.
Your email looks unprofessional: create a new one using your name, which takes five minutes.

body.text: Practice
Rewrite the top third today, and tailor it once.

items: Copy the job title from one advert into your headline.
Rewrite the summary in two lines, with one fact in it.
Delete three lines from the list above.
Move the most relevant job to the top.
Export as a PDF and open it on a phone.

body.text: You can now write a page that gets finished. In the next lesson you will prepare for an interview that happens through a screen.

excerpt: Preparing a video interview: the setup that takes ten minutes, the answers to rehearse, and the small habits that carry a conversation.

body.text: This lesson prepares you for an interview on a screen: the setup, the answers to rehearse, and the small habits that make a video call feel like a conversation. You will test everything the day before, not ten minutes before.
A video interview is an ordinary interview with an extra risk: the connection, the light, and the sound. Remove those three risks and the conversation is the same as any other.
Before you start

items: The interview time, in both time zones if the employer is abroad.
A phone or laptop with a working camera and microphone.
A quiet place with a plain background.
One day to test, and one hour to prepare.

body.text: The setup, tested early

items: Sit with a window in front of you, never behind, so your face is lit.
Put the camera at eye level, on books if needed.
Test the microphone by recording yourself for thirty seconds and listening.
Use headphones when the room echoes, which it usually does.
Charge the device, and have a second one ready with the same link.
Ask somebody to call you on the same app at the same hour, as a rehearsal.

body.text: You will see your own face in a small box, and the interviewer in the large one. Look at the camera when you speak, rather than at the face on the screen.

body.alt: A laptop propped on books with a window in front and headphones beside it.
body.caption: Camera at eye level, window in front, headphones ready. Ten minutes of setup removes most of the risk.

body.text: It looks like a video interview is less formal than a face-to-face one. It is recorded more often, and small habits show more clearly on a screen.
The answers to rehearse

items: Tell me about yourself, in ninety seconds, ending at why you want this job.
Why this company, in two sentences that mention something specific.
A problem you solved, in the order: situation, action, result.
A mistake you made, and what you changed afterwards.
What you would do in the first month, in three steps.
Your questions for them, at least two, written down.

body.text: Rehearsal will feel strange for the first two attempts and normal by the fourth. Say the answers aloud, since reading them silently builds no memory at all.
The screen will show the interviewer a second before their voice arrives, which is normal on a slow connection. Wait for the sound, then answer, rather than speaking over the pause.

body.alt: A person speaking in a video interview with notes beside the laptop.
body.caption: Notes beside the camera, not under it. Glancing down is normal, and reading a script aloud is not.

body.text: During the call

items: Join five minutes early, and wait in the lobby rather than messaging.
Greet them by name, and thank them for the time in the first sentence.
Keep answers to about a minute, then stop, which leaves room for a question.
Nod and say a short yes rather than staying silent while they speak.
Have your CV open beside the window, not on the same screen.
Ask your two questions before the end, even if everything is answered.

body.text: None of this needs a suit or a studio. A plain shirt, a tidy wall, and clear sound are what the interviewer notices.
Do not worry about a child or a fan in the background. Say sorry once, and continue, since composure under a small interruption is itself an answer.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a fix you can apply without leaving the call.

items: The connection drops: rejoin at once, and message the interviewer if the link fails twice.
The sound fails: type in the chat, then switch to a phone call.
You cannot hear them: say so in the first minute, rather than guessing at the questions.
You froze on a question: ask them to repeat it, which buys ten seconds and looks normal.
The camera shows you from below: raise the laptop, and carry on.
The call runs out of time: ask for an email address and send your two questions afterwards.

body.text: Practice
Record one answer and watch it once.

items: Set the laptop on books and open a window in front of you.
Record the ninety-second answer on your phone.
Watch it once, and note two things to change.
Record it again, and keep the second version.
Write your two questions for the employer.

body.text: You can now be interviewed across a screen without losing the room. In the next lesson you will make slides that help a talk instead of replacing it.

excerpt: Making slides that support a talk: one idea per slide, big type, few words, and the practice that stops a presentation being read aloud.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to make slides that help a talk. You will use one idea per slide, large type, and few words, and you will practise so the slides support you rather than replace you.
A slide is a support for a person speaking. If the slide says everything, the audience reads it and stops listening, and the speaker becomes unnecessary.
Before you start

items: A talk you must give, or one you could give.
A slide program, though paper works while planning.
About an hour.

body.text: Plan on paper first

items: Write the one sentence the audience must remember.
Break it into three points, and no more.
Give each point one slide.
Add a first slide with the title and your name.
Add a last slide with the action you want them to take.
Count the slides: five is a talk, and twenty-five is a document.

body.text: You will see the whole talk on one piece of paper, which is the only way to notice a missing step. Planning inside the slide program hides the shape of the argument.

body.alt: A slide with a large heading and three short lines of text.
body.caption: A heading you can read from the back row, and three short lines. Anything smaller belongs in your mouth, not on the screen.

body.text: It looks like a slide with more detail is more helpful. The audience cannot read and listen at once, and the reading always wins.
Type, colour, and space

items: Use a heading of at least forty points, and body text of at least twenty-four.
Use one font family, and two colours plus black and white.
Keep the background plain, since a patterned background fights the text.
Put no more than six short lines on a slide.
Use a picture when it explains something faster than a sentence.
Leave a wide margin, which makes the slide look calm.

body.text: The slide will look sparse on a laptop screen, and that is correct. It is designed for a projector and a person at the back of a room.

On the projector, the headings will look larger than they did on the laptop, which is the reason to check one slide in the room. If a heading is hard to read from the back row, everything else is too small.

body.alt: A person presenting with slides on a large screen behind them.
body.caption: The speaker is the presentation. The screen carries the three points, and the room watches both.

body.text: Practising the talk

items: Say the talk aloud three times, with the slides in front of you.
Time yourself, and cut a point if you run over.
Practise the first minute twice as much as the rest.
Note where you look at the screen instead of the room.
Prepare one sentence for a question you fear.
Take a printed copy of the slides, in case the projector fails.

body.text: None of this needs a rehearsal room. A kitchen and a timer are enough, and three run-throughs remove most of the nerves.
Do not worry about forgetting a line. The slide in front of you holds the heading, and the heading is the cue.
If it goes wrong
Every case here happens at real talks, and each has a response ready.

items: The projector fails: use the printed copy, and keep talking, which the room prefers.
The slides will not open: present from a PDF, which opens anywhere.
You run out of time: skip to the last slide, and say what you are skipping.
A question you cannot answer: say you will find out, and ask for an email address.
The room cannot read the text: read the heading aloud, and move on.
You speak too fast: pause after each slide, which slows the whole talk.

body.text: Practice
Build five slides for a three-minute talk.

items: Write the one sentence the audience must remember.
Give each of the three points one slide.
Set the heading to forty points and check it from across the room.
Add a first and a last slide.
Say it aloud three times with a timer.

body.text: You can now speak with slides rather than behind them. In the next lesson you will write an email that gets an answer.
